strengths: Novel and mathematically rigorous theoretical framework: embedding arbitrary planar (and more generally crystallographic) groups into affine reflection supergroups and applying a Hironaka-type primary/secondary invariant decomposition to construct continuous, boundary-discontinuity-free G-invariant representations. This cleanly solves a real problem (naive asymmetric-unit extension breaks continuity for non-reflective symmetry operations).

Strong theoretical completeness: the appendix proves existence/non-existence of the required affine-reflection embedding for general n (with explicit group-theoretic counterexamples for n>3, n≠7,8, and delicate constructions for n=7,8), giving the main text's Thm. 3.2/3.3 a solid foundation rather than leaving it as a conjecture.

Practical, efficient computational recipe: Table 2 and the Fourier/Chebyshev-based derivation give an explicit, implementable basis for all 17 planar groups, and the method has O(n^2) per-pixel cost versus O(n^6)/O(n^4) for a basis-projection alternative, which is empirically and analytically justified in App. A.2.

Broad empirical validation across four heterogeneous tasks (RGB pattern design, paper-cutting with physical fabrication verification, topology optimization with mechanical objectives, and metamaterial zero-shot symmetry transfer), showing the representation genuinely decouples symmetry enforcement from task-specific losses and generalizes beyond a single application.

Reasonable baselines and ablations: comparison against strong MLLMs (direct/conditional/post-symmetrization settings), against a basis-projection symmetrization baseline at multiple resolutions, and against a CLIP-loss topology-optimization baseline, with quantitative (CLIP-A, MSE, bulk modulus, volume MAE) and qualitative results.
Extensive, detailed experimental/implementation appendix (hyperparameters, loss schedules, dataset construction, FEA/homogenization settings) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies heavily on CLIP-A as an aesthetic proxy and pixel MSE for symmetry fidelity; there is no human/user study or diversity metric to assess whether the generated 'strictly symmetric' patterns are perceptually appealing or diverse beyond a handful of qualitative figures.

The comparison protocol against MLLMs (fitting a symmetric representation to a non-symmetric MLLM output via MSE, i.e., 'post-symmetrization') is somewhat contrived: it does not test whether MLLMs could produce better symmetric outputs under a different constraint mechanism, so the resulting comparison partly restates the known fact that unconstrained generative models are not exactly symmetric rather than isolating the proposed representation's advantage.

The core theoretical apparatus (invariant theory, Hironaka decomposition, classification results for n>3) is very heavy relative to the practical scope of the paper (which experiments only with n=2); the significant mathematical investment in n=3,7,8 results, while intellectually interesting, is not exercised experimentally, leaving its practical payoff unclear within this submission.

Fairness of some head-to-head comparisons (e.g., topology design vs. Zhong et al. baseline, paper-cutting vs. projection baseline) is asserted via 'identical hyperparameters' but the loss weighting schedules and step counts sometimes differ between baseline and proposed method (e.g., §F.3 lists different optimization step counts and CFG schedules for baseline vs. ours), which could confound the reported gains.

Limitations of the method itself are not clearly discussed in the main text (e.g., approximation error from finite secondary-invariant truncation, sensitivity to hash-grid resolution, or cases where task losses conflict with the fixed symmetric parameterization); the conclusion section is largely a restatement of contributions without a dedicated limitations discussion.
The abstract states 'Code is available at' with no URL provided in the visible text, raising a minor reproducibility/transparency concern despite the otherwise detailed appendix.

strengths: Provides a rigorous mathematical framework (based on affine reflection group embeddings and Hironaka/invariant-theoretic decomposition) for symmetrizing arbitrary continuous 2D representations under any of the 17 planar groups while provably preserving continuity, resolving the boundary-discontinuity problem of naive asymmetric-unit extension for non-reflective symmetry elements.

Theoretical contribution is unusually deep and complete for a generative-modeling paper: existence/non-existence proofs for higher reflectional supergroups in general dimension n (including the subtle exceptional cases n=7,8), explicit Hironaka decomposition machinery, and an approximation guarantee (Thm 3.3/C.12) that the construction can approximate any G-invariant function arbitrarily well.

The framework is demonstrated as genuinely unifying: the same symmetrization module plugs into four distinct downstream tasks (pattern design, paper-cutting, topology design, metamaterial design) purely by changing task-specific loss terms (SDS, VTM connectivity loss, homogenization-based mechanical loss), without needing symmetry-specific training data or retrained generators.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: comparisons against strong/recent MLLM baselines and a basis-projection baseline with quantitative metrics (CLIP-A, MSE) across all 17 groups, an efficiency/complexity analysis of alternative symmetrization strategies, and a physical paper-cutting fabrication demonstrating real-world manufacturability.

The topology/metamaterial experiments meaningfully extend the idea beyond pure visual generation to physically constrained design (homogenization-based bulk modulus maximization, virtual temperature method for connectivity), showing the representation's utility for engineering-relevant symmetry control in a zero-shot setting.

Extensive appendix with full proofs, computation recipes (Table 2 of secondary invariants for all 17 groups), and detailed experimental/hyperparameter documentation supports reproducibility of the theoretical and empirical claims.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation relies mainly on CLIP-A aesthetic scores and MSE against self-generated symmetrized references; there is no human perceptual study or task-specific quality metric (e.g., manufacturability rate beyond a few hand-crafted paper-cutting examples), which are weak proxies for whether the generated patterns are genuinely useful/appealing to designers.

Comparisons to MLLM baselines (GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro) use a 'post-symmetrization' protocol that projects the baseline's output onto the authors' own symmetric representation before computing MSE; this evaluation is somewhat self-referential (baseline error is measured through the proposed method's own fitting procedure) and may not fully isolate the intrinsic contribution of the representation versus the evaluation protocol.

Topology-design and metamaterial results are largely qualitative/visual (Figs. 7-8, 14-16) with limited statistical rigor (no variance/significance testing across seeds beyond box plots), and hyperparameters (loss weights, annealing schedules, volume-fraction thresholds) appear to be heavily and separately tuned per task, raising concerns about sensitivity and generalizability without careful re-tuning for new domains.

The core theoretical machinery (Hironaka decomposition, GL(n,Q) conjugacy classes, root-system classification) is highly specialized commutative-algebra/representation-theory content; although rigorous, it is dense and largely pushed into a 30-page appendix, making the paper's true technical contribution difficult for a typical ICML reader to verify without substantial background, and the main text's exposition of why this machinery is necessary (vs. simpler heuristics) could be more self-contained.

The guaranteed exact continuous symmetrization construction is only established for n ≤ 3 (where an affine reflection supergroup always exists); for higher-dimensional periodic structures (n>3, excluding special low-rank coincidences) the method's core theoretical guarantee provably fails, which restricts applicability beyond planar/3D space groups despite the paper's framing as a general n-dimensional theory.

Related-work coverage in the main paper is brief, with substantive discussion of alternative symmetrization strategies and closely related metamaterial/crystal generation work (e.g., Mao et al. 2020) deferred to the appendix, making it harder to assess the paper's incremental novelty relative to prior symmetry-constrained generative design methods from the main text alone.
